1.note: The pronoun **he** refers to the one whom Ezekiel saw sitting on the throne, as described in the chapter 1. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers as in the UST. While it is assumed that this is Yahweh, he is not specifically named.

Yahweh is using **son of man** as a common expression of the culture to mean “human being.” See the Introduction to Ezekiel for more information on this form of address. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly as in the UST. See how you translated “Son of man” in [2:1](ta:02). This also occurs in verses 3, 4, 10, 17, and 25.

Eating the scroll was a symbolic action by which Ezekiel showed that he was taking Yahweh’s message completely into himself so that he could speak it to others. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in a footnote.

Here, **house** means all the people descended from a particular person. It envisions them as if they were one household living together. So **the house of Israel** means all the people descended from the patriarch Jacob, who was also known as Israel. This also occurs in verses 4, 5, 7, and 17. Alternate translation: [the people of Israel]

3.q: בִּטְנְ⁠ךָ֤ תַֽאֲכֵל֙ וּ⁠מֵעֶ֣י⁠ךָ תְמַלֵּ֔א אֵ֚ת הַ⁠מְּגִלָּ֣ה הַ⁠זֹּ֔את אֲשֶׁ֥ר אֲנִ֖י נֹתֵ֣ן אֵלֶ֑י⁠ךָ
3.note: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Alternate translation: [you shall completely fill your stomach with that scroll that I am giving to you]

The point of this comparison is that just as **honey** is sweet and pleasant to eat, so the scroll that Ezekiel ate was pleasant to him. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [as pleasant to eat as sweet honey]

4.note: See how you translated the same phrase, “the house of Israel” in [verse 1](ta:01). Alternate translation: [the people of Israel]

5.note: Yahweh is using **deep of lip** and **heavy of tongue** as common expressions of the culture to refer to speaking a language that is unfamiliar and difficult to understand. If these phrases do not have that meaning for your readers, you could use comparable expressions from your language that do have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [foreigners whose speech is unfamiliar and have a language that you cannot understand]

The expression **are you being sent** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [do I send you]
See how you translated the same phrase, “the house of Israel” in [verse 1](ta:01). Alternate translation: [the people of Israel]

6.note: Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [I am not sending you to one of the many foreign people groups]
See how you translated these same phrases, “deep of lip” and “heavy of tongue”, in the previous verse. Alternate translation: [who speak difficult languages you cannot understand]

Yahweh is using **do not hear their words** as a common expression of the culture to mean “do not understand what they say.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [with whom you cannot communicate]

Yahweh is stating the pronoun **they** separately, even though the expression **they would have listened** already includes this meaning. He is doing that because he is contrasting what these peoples would have done with what the Israelites will do. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing that meaning here. Alternate translation: [If I had sent you to them, they would have listened to you]

Here, **listen** means to intentionally hear and obey. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [they would have listened to and obeyed what you told them to do]

7.note: See how you translated the phrase used twice here, “house of Israel” in [verse 1](ta:01). Alternate translation: [But the people of Israel]

Yahweh is using **strong of forehead** and **hard of heart** as common expressions of the culture to mean “stubborn” and “unwilling to obey.” If these phrases do not have that meaning for your readers, you could use comparable expressions from your language that do have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they are stubborn and refuse to obey]

8.note: Yahweh is using the term **Behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [Listen carefully]

8.q: נָתַ֧תִּי אֶת־פָּנֶ֛י⁠ךָ חֲזָקִ֖ים לְ⁠עֻמַּ֣ת פְּנֵי⁠הֶ֑ם וְ⁠אֶֽת־מִצְחֲ⁠ךָ֥ חָזָ֖ק לְ⁠עֻמַּ֥ת מִצְחָֽ⁠ם
8.note: Yahweh is using **your face strong** and **your forehead hard** as common expressions of the culture to mean that he has made Ezekiel just as determined and unyielding as the people of Israel are. If these phrases do not have that meaning for your readers, you could use comparable expressions from your language that do have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I have made you just as determined as they are and just as unyielding as they are]

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and I have made your forehead]

9.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **a thorn harder than flint** cannot be broken, so Ezekiel will not be broken by the opposition of the people of Israel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [I have made you as strong and unyielding as stone]

A **flint** is a kind of very hard stone. If your readers would not be familiar with what flint is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [than a very hard stone]
See how you translated the similar phrase “your forehead hard” in 3:8.
See how you translated these very similar phrases, “you shall not fear; and from their faces you shall not be dismayed, for they are a house of rebellion” in 2:6.

10.note: Here Yahweh is speaking of the **heart**, which represents where a person’s thoughts and emotions exist, as if they were a container into which he could put the words that Yahweh speaks. You may have a comparable expression in your language, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [consider them carefully]

Yahweh is using **in your ears** and **listen** together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [and listen to and obey them carefully]

11.note: In this verse, the word **the exile** is singular in form, but it refers to all the Israelites who were exiled to Babylon as a group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural form of “the exile.” Alternate translation: [the exiles]

Yahweh is speaking of the Israelites as if they were the **sons** of their ancestors. He uses it this way to remind Ezekiel that these are his own people. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your own countrymen]

11.q: וְ⁠אָמַרְתָּ֣ אֲלֵי⁠הֶ֔ם כֹּ֥ה אָמַ֖ר אֲדֹנָ֣⁠י יְהֹוִ֑ה
11.note: Yahweh is instructing Ezekiel, **and you shall say to them, ‘Thus says the Lord Yahweh,’** to indicate that what he is telling Ezekiel to say comes with Yahweh’s authority. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating the authoritative source of direct quotations in your language. See how you translated this same expression in 2:4.
See how you translated the same expression, “whether they listen or whether they refuse,” in 2:5.

12.note: The implication is that the words of this blessing are what the loud rumbling sounded like it was saying. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [it sounded like it said, “Blessed be the glory of Yahweh from his place]

The expression **Blessed be** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [May everyone bless the glory of Yahweh from his place]
If your language does not use a noun for the idea of **glory**, you could express the same idea in another way as in the UST.

13.note: Ezekiel is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and I heard the sound of the wings of the living beings]
See how you translated the similar phrase “were each joining to its sister” in 1:9. Alternate translation: [each brushing the wing next to it]

14.note: Ezekiel is using **the heat of my spirit** as a common expression of the culture to mean “feeling angry.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I went away feeling angry and distressed]

Here, **the hand of Yahweh** represents “the power of Yahweh.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and the power of Yahweh was strong on me]

15.note: In this verse, the word **exile** is singular in form, but it refers to all the Israelites who were exiled to Babylon as a group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural form of “exile.” Alternate translation: [the exiles]
The word **Tel Aviv** means “mound of the flood” and here describes a town that is a different place than the modern day city with that name.

16.note: Ezekiel is using the words translated as **And it was** to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.

Ezekiel uses **the word of Yahweh** to represent the message that Yahweh spoke. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the message that Yahweh spoke was]
The term **saying** introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this term explicitly.

17.note: Here Yahweh is speaking as if Ezekiel were **a watchman**, that is, a lookout stationed on a city wall to warn the people of approaching danger. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I have made you the one to warn the house of Israel of coming danger]

Here, **house** means all the people descended from a particular person. It envisions them as if they were one household living together. So **the house of Israel** figuratively means all the people descended from the patriarch Jacob, who was also known as Israel. Alternate translation: [for the people of Israel]
Here, **a word from my mouth** represents “what I say.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [what I say]
The pronoun **it** refers to the word that Ezekiel hears from Yahweh. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and you shall warn them with that word]

18.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [When I tell the wicked person that he will certainly die,]

Yahweh is using the adjective **wicked** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [any wicked person]

Yahweh is using the adjective **wicked** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [to warn the wicked person from his wicked way]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if a person’s manner of living were a **way**, that is, a road or path on which the person travels. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. This also occurs in verse 19. Alternate translation: [about his wicked behavior]

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [so that he might leave his wicked way and live]

Yahweh is stating the pronoun **he** separately, even though the verb translated as **he will die** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that it is the wicked person himself, and not the watchman, who will die for his sin. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [that wicked person himself will die]

Yahweh is using **his blood from your hand I will seek** as a common expression of the culture to mean “I will hold you responsible for his death.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. This also occurs in verse 20. Alternate translation: [but I will consider you guilty of his death]

19.note: Yahweh is stating the pronoun **you** separately, even though the verb translated as **you warn** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize the watchman’s own responsibility when he does give the warning, in contrast with the previous verse, where the watchman failed to warn the wicked person. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [But when you do warn]

Yahweh is using the adjective **wicked** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [that wicked person]

Here Yahweh is speaking of a person who would not stop behaving wickedly as if he would not **turn from** following **his wicked way** as if it were a road on which he had been traveling. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he does not stop his wickedness or his wicked behavior]
If your language does not use a noun for the idea of **wickedness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [from acting wickedly]

Yahweh is stating the pronoun **he** separately, even though the verb translated as **he will die** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that he is sure to die if he does not turn from his wicked way. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [he himself will die]

Yahweh is stating the pronoun **you** separately, even though the verb translated as **you will have rescued** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that Ezekiel himself will not be held guilty for the wicked person’s death, since he warned him, in contrast to what happens to the wicked person who refuses to turn from his sin. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [but you will have rescued your own life]

The implication is that Ezekiel will have **rescued** his own life if he warns the wicked person so that he will not be considered responsible for the death of the wicked person. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. This also occurs in verse 21. Alternate translation: [you will have rescued your own life from being held responsible for his death]

20.note: Yahweh is using the adjective **righteous** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [a righteous person]

Ezekiel is speaking of a righteous person ceasing to do what is right as if that person would **turn** away from the right path. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [But when the righteous person stops doing what is right]
If your language does not use a noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [from doing what is right]
If your language does not use a noun for the idea of **injustice**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [acts unjustly]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if a disaster for a person were **a stumbling-block** placed in his path on which the person would trip and fall. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and I cause a disaster to happen to him]

Yahweh is stating the pronoun **he** separately, even though the verb translated as **he will die** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that this person will certainly die because of his own sin. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [he will certainly die]

The expression **will not be remember** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and I will not consider the righteous things that he did]
See how you translated this same phrase, “but his blood from your hand I will seek,” in verse 18. Alternate translation: [but I will consider you guilty of his death]

21.note: Yahweh is stating the pronoun **you** separately, even though the verb translated as **you warn** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that the contrast with the other scenarios. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [But if you yourself warn him]

Ezekiel is using the adjective **righteous** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [that righteous person]

By **without sinning is the righteous** Yahweh means that the righteous should not keep sinning. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [that those who are righteous should stop sinning]

Yahweh is stating the pronoun **he** separately, even though the verb translated as **he does not sin** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that it is the righteous person himself whose own conduct determines whether he lives. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [and he does not sin anymore]

By **his life will be** Yahweh means he will not die because he has chosen to stop sinning. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [his life will continue]

The expression **he was warned** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [because you warned him]
See how you translated these same phrases in verse 19.

22.note: Ezekiel is using the word translated as **So** to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.
See how you translated the similar expression, “on him there, the hand of Yahweh,” in 1:3.

23.note: Ezekiel is using the term **behold** to focus his readers’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [and look!]

23.q: כְּבוֹד־יְהוָה֙ עֹמֵ֔ד כַּ⁠כָּב֕וֹד אֲשֶׁ֥ר רָאִ֖יתִי עַל־נְהַר־כְּבָ֑ר וָ⁠אֶפֹּ֖ל עַל־פָּנָֽ⁠י
23.note: See how you translated the similar phrases, “the likeness of the glory of Yahweh. And I saw, and I fell to my face,” in 1:28.

24.q: וַ⁠תָּבֹא־בִ֣⁠י ר֔וּחַ וַ⁠תַּעֲמִדֵ֖⁠נִי עַל־רַגְלָ֑⁠י וַ⁠יְדַבֵּ֤ר אֹתִ⁠י֙ וַ⁠יֹּ֣אמֶר אֵלַ֔⁠י
24.note: See how you translated the similar phrases, “the Spirit entered into me when he spoke to me, and it made me stand on my feet,” in 2:2.
The pronoun **he** refers to Yahweh who is the one whom Ezekiel saw sitting on the throne, as described in the 1:28. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers as in the UST.

The term **saying** introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this term explicitly as in the UST, since this is clear from the word **spoke.**

25.note: Ezekiel is using the term **behold** to focus his listeners’ attention on what he is about to say. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation. Alternate translation: [hear this!]

The pronoun **They** refers to the exiles from Israel among whom Ezekiel was living. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [The people you are living among will put ropes on you]

26.note: Here, **your tongue** represents Ezekiel’s ability to speak. By saying that it will **cling to your palate,** Yahweh is declaring that Ezekiel will not be able to speak for a time. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [And I will take away your ability to speak]

Yahweh is using **to a man** as a common expression of his culture to mean “each person.” If this phrase does not have that meaning in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to each person]
See how you translated the same phrase, “a house of rebellion” in 2:5.

27.note: Yahweh uses the word **And** here to indicate a contrast. While Ezekiel was told in the previous verse that he would not be able to speak to the people to reprove them as he’d been assigned to do, he is now told that will only be until Yahweh gives him a message to speak to them. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [But when I speak]

Yahweh is using **I will open your mouth** as a common expression of the culture to mean “I will enable you to speak.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will enable you to speak]

27.q: וְ⁠אָמַרְתָּ֣ אֲלֵי⁠הֶ֔ם כֹּ֥ה אָמַ֖ר אֲדֹנָ֣⁠י יְהֹוִ֑ה
27.note: Yahweh is instructing Ezekiel, **and you will say to them, ‘Thus says the Lord Yahweh!’** to indicate that what he is telling Ezekiel to say comes with Yahweh’s authority. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating the authoritative source of direct quotations in your language. See how you translated this same expression in 2:4.

Ezekiel is repeating forms of the verbs **hearing** and **refusing** in order to intensify his expression of the ideas that they convey. See how you translated the repeated phrase with the similar wording, “whether they listen or whether they refuse,” in 2:5. Alternate translation: [The one who hears this message will listen and obey it, but the one who refuses to hear it will keep on refusing]
See how you translated the similar phrase, “a house of rebellion” in 2:5.
